c.tagline: Mexico's soul of mezcal, mole, and Zapotec craft, wrapped around a golden colonial core.

taxi.color: varies (often white and red, or blue)
taxi.fareNote: Oaxaca street taxis are unmetered; agree the fare before getting in, or use Uber/DiDi to see the price up front.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified nationwide emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance.

hood_landmark.Centro Histórico: Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Oaxaca

avoid.reason: Generally safe; occasional protests/road blockades; petty crime at night

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed colonial core around the Zócalo and the Santo Domingo church, packed with markets, mezcalerías, museums, and most of the city's sights; the best all-around base for a first visit.
A hip, artsy barrio of cobblestone streets, street art, colorful facades, coffee shops, and mezcal bars just a 10-minute walk from the Zócalo; the favorite of couples and creative travelers.
One of the oldest neighborhoods in Latin America, a quieter cultural quarter of aqueduct arches, artisan workshops, and small plazas; ideal for a slower, more local pace.
A largely residential, authentic district just west of Centro where daily life carries on with little thought for tourism; cheaper stays and still a 10-15 minute walk to the Zócalo.
A traditional, budget-friendly barrio south of Centro near the Basílica de la Soledad, with local markets and family-run eateries and fewer crowds.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water; tap water is not potable.

transit.hours: City buses (urbanos) and colectivos run roughly 5:30 AM to 10:00 PM; after that, taxis and ride apps fill the gap.
transit.note: Oaxaca has no metro or tram; the compact Centro is best explored on foot, with city buses, shared colectivo taxis, and app or street taxis for longer hops.
transit.pay: Bus and colectivo fares are paid in cash to the driver (roughly 9-12 pesos); there is no rechargeable transit card.

bus: ADO / OCC / AU first-class intercity buses
Colectivos to the Valles Centrales villages

transit.m: Prepaid airport taxi to Centro (buy the ticket at the kiosk inside; 20-25 min, zone-based fare)
Shared colectivo van (transportación terrestre) to Centro

tip.r: 10-15% is standard at restaurants; round up for taxis and leave a little for hotel and tour staff.

food.name: Mole negro
food.desc: Oaxaca's most famous of seven moles: chilhuacle chillies, charred seeds, spices and chocolate cooked into a near-black sauce over turkey or chicken.

places.name: Casa Oaxaca El Restaurante
places.note: Rooftop dining room that made refined Oaxacan cooking internationally known.

places.name: Los Danzantes
places.note: Courtyard restaurant pairing moles with its own mezcal label.

places.name: Levadura de Olla
places.note: Chef Thalia Barrios' kitchen cooking moles over wood fire from village recipes.

food.name: Tlayudas
food.desc: A huge crisp corn tortilla spread with bean paste and asiento pork lard, topped with quesillo, cabbage and grilled meat, then folded over the coals.

places.name: Tlayudas Libres
places.note: Late-night charcoal tlayuda stand that locals treat as the standard-bearer.

places.name: Tlayudas Dona Martha
places.note: Long-running neighbourhood spot cooking tlayudas over wood into the small hours.

places.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: Market comedores serving tlayudas through the day at low prices.

food.name: Chapulines
food.desc: Grasshoppers toasted with garlic, lime and chilli, eaten by the handful or piled onto tlayudas and guacamole; a pre-Hispanic Oaxacan staple.

places.name: Mercado Benito Juarez
places.note: Rows of vendors selling chapulines graded by size; free tastes before buying.

places.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: Comedores serve chapulines as a botana with mezcal and fresh tortillas.

places.name: Casa Oaxaca El Restaurante
places.note: Works chapulines into modern dishes for those wanting a gentler introduction.

food.name: Quesillo and memelas
food.desc: Stringy Oaxacan cheese pulled into a ball, melted onto thick hand-pressed memelas smeared with bean paste and salsa.

places.name: Itanoni
places.note: Tortilleria devoted to native corn varieties; the best memelas in the city.

places.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: Market stalls griddle memelas and quesadillas to order all morning.

places.name: La Cosecha Organic Market
places.note: Small food hall with masa-based antojitos made from regional corn.

food.name: Tasajo and cecina from the Pasillo de Humo
food.desc: Thin salted beef and chilli-rubbed pork grilled over charcoal in a smoke-filled market corridor, eaten with tortillas, onion and salsa.

places.name: Pasillo de Humo, Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: The smoke alley itself: pick your meat, they grill it, you eat standing.

places.name: Mercado de la Merced
places.note: Quieter local market with the same grilled-meat comedores and better prices.

places.name: Mercado de Abastos
places.note: Sprawling wholesale market with a large Saturday grilled-meat section.

food.name: Tamales oaxaquenos
food.desc: Masa spread with mole negro and chicken, wrapped in banana leaf rather than corn husk and steamed until soft and glossy.

places.name: Zandunga
places.note: Isthmus-of-Tehuantepec kitchen with a strong tamal and regional dish list.

places.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: Morning tamal vendors sell out before mid-day; go early.

places.name: La Cosecha Organic Market
places.note: Producer stalls with banana-leaf tamales alongside atole.

food.name: Tejate
food.desc: Pre-Hispanic cold drink of maize, cacao, mamey seed and cacao flower, hand-whipped until a pale foam rises and served from clay bowls.

places.name: Mercado Benito Juarez
places.note: Several tejateras whipping bowls by hand right in the market aisles.

places.name: Mercado 20 de Noviembre
places.note: Easy first taste of tejate alongside aguas frescas and chocolate.

places.name: San Andres Huayapam tejate stands
places.note: The village credited with tejate, 20 minutes out; the benchmark version.

food.name: Mezcal
food.desc: Wood-roasted agave distilled in village palenques across Oaxaca; sipped neat with orange and sal de gusano, never shot.

places.name: In Situ Mezcaleria
places.note: Ulises Torrentera's bar, the most respected mezcal reference room in Oaxaca.

places.name: Mezcaloteca
places.note: Appointment-only tasting library focused on traceable small-producer mezcal.

places.name: Sabina Sabe
places.note: Lively cocktail bar using mezcal creatively; good if you want mixed drinks.

landmarks: Monte Albán
The mountaintop Zapotec capital, a UNESCO city of pyramids, ballcourts and carved Danzantes flattened onto a ridge above the valley.
Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán
A baroque marvel whose gilded interior drips with golden foliage, fronting a plaza that anchors Oaxaca's most beautiful street.
Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución)
Oaxaca's laurel-shaded main square hums with marimba bands, café terraces and vendors beneath the arcades and cathedral towers.
Museo de las Culturas de Oaxaca
In Santo Domingo's former monastery, this superb museum crowns its cloisters with the golden Mixtec treasure of Monte Albán's Tomb 7.
Árbol del Tule
A two-thousand-year-old Montezuma cypress in Santa María del Tule boasts the world's stoutest trunk, dwarfing the church beside it.
Mitla Archaeological Site
The Zapotec 'place of the dead' dazzles with palaces sheathed in intricate geometric stone fretwork found nowhere else in Mesoamerica.
Mercados Benito Juárez and 20 de Noviembre
Adjoining markets overflow with mole pastes, chapulines, mezcal and the legendary smoke-filled grilled-meat alley, Oaxaca's gastronomic heart.
Jardín Etnobotánico de Oaxaca
A stunning garden of cacti, agaves and native flora arranged like living sculpture within Santo Domingo's old monastery walls.
Basílica de Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
Oaxaca's patroness resides in this seventeenth-century baroque basilica, its carved stone facade rising like a folding screen above a sloping plaza.
Cerro del Fortín
A hill just west of the Zócalo reached by a long stairway, topped by an open-air auditorium and panoramic views over the city and Monte Albán.

train.note: Mexico has no intercity passenger rail serving Oaxaca. The Interoceánico corridor across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec has begun limited passenger operation well to the south of the city, but there is nothing from Oaxaca itself. Travel is by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. ADO (https://www.ado.com.mx/) runs from the first-class terminal north of the centre to Mexico City in about 6 hours on the toll road, plus Puebla, Veracruz and San Cristóbal de las Casas (10-11 hours overnight). Second-class buses and vans to Puerto Escondido and the coast leave from smaller terminals and take 6-7 hours on a winding mountain road.

ferry.note: Oaxaca city sits in a highland valley about 250 km from the Pacific with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. Boat trips run from the coastal towns of Puerto Escondido and Huatulco as excursions.

full.blurb: Mineral springs and petrified 'frozen' waterfalls with cliff-edge natural infinity pools, about 1.5-2 hours southeast in the Sierra.
full.name: Hierve el Agua

full.blurb: Zapotec ruins famous for intricate stone-mosaic fretwork, paired with a nearby village of traditional wool-rug weavers and mezcal palenques.
full.name: Mitla & Teotitlán del Valle

half.blurb: Village home to El Árbol del Tule, a roughly 2,000-year-old cypress with one of the widest trunks of any tree on earth.
half.name: Santa María del Tule
